name: Sam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a shuttle car at the potash mine, six hundred metres under the plains. The cutting machine chews the ore off the face, loads it into my car, and I run it back to the feeder and dump it, back and forth all shift. I've been there just under two years. Before that I milked cows on the Hendriks dairy for twenty years, until old Hendriks sold up and the new owners put in a milking robot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work and it pays the mortgage, which the dairy barely did. The men are good, a few of them go to my church. Hard is that I'm still learning, I bumped the rib side twice in the first month and I've not lived it down. And Ruth's job at the bakery is mornings only, so it's my pay that carries us, and there's nothing left over at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd say it with a grin. I never believed a computer was going to come down a mine shaft. I'd say it at work and after church, I don't go on the internet for that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, same thing. It means I keep driving and keep my head down. I've seen one robot take a job already, at the dairy, but that was a milking machine, not some clever brain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Go to work, come home, fix what needs fixing round the house. Maybe ask the shift boss what I need to do to get off the junior rate. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff, I don't see what it'd do for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the milking robot. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day it went in, Hendriks's son walked me round it like it was a new calf. It cost more than my house. Two weeks later they didn't need me, and they were decent about it, gave me a month's pay, but it was still a robot that sent me home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that change how you'd feel about this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd still watch the machines more than the computers. But in this picture nothing big happens, so I'd let it lie.

S0.say: He'd say I told you so with a grin, at work and after church, as he never believed a computer would come down a mine shaft.
S0.think: Privately he agrees: he keeps driving and keeps his head down. He's already lost a job to a milking robot, but sees that as machinery rather than AI.
S0.do: Carries on as usual and asks the shift boss how to move off the junior pay rate. Avoids AI tools entirely.
S0.quote: Two weeks later they didn't need me, and they were decent about it, gave me a month's pay, but it was still a robot that sent me home.
S0.fieldNote: Sam has already lost a job to a robot, yet he treats AI and machines as different things. In the calm picture he sees no reason to change anything. Church and his crew are where he talks, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has the right to run its business, but a good company looks after its men. I'd say the old way of doing things had something to it. And I'd say we don't need the government making it worse with more rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the shuttle cars go remote or automatic before long, they're simple runs. I've got two years in and the junior rate, so I'm the first name on the list. It's the dairy again, only I've got a mortgage this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten the belt straight off, no eating out, no new tyres till the old ones are bald. I'd try to put something away every pay, even if it's small. And I'd wait to see what the company does before I go chasing courses, because I'm not going to throw money at something that doesn't lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in the shoulders that doesn't let up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Some of your workmates might start retraining right away. What would you think of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good on them, I'd say. It's not for me, I'm not a classroom man and I'm not going to start at forty-three. I'd rather be the one they keep because he never misses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Caleb to get a trade, a real one, electrician or plumber, something with his hands and his head. He's fifteen and he wants to work at the mine like his dad. I'd tell him not to, and that would hurt to say.

S1.say: He'd say the company has the right to run its business but should look after its workers, that the old way had merit, and that more government rules would make things worse.
S1.think: He thinks the shuttle cars will soon be automated and, as a junior worker, he'll be first to go. It feels like the dairy again, but now with a mortgage.
S1.do: Cuts spending straight away and tries to save something every pay. Waits to see what the company offers before paying for any course, aiming to be kept for his reliability.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a tightness in his shoulders.
S1.quote: He's fifteen and he wants to work at the mine like his dad. I'd tell him not to, and that would hurt to say.
S1.fieldNote: Sam's traditional values show in defending the company's right to automate while expecting it to care for its workers. He won't retrain himself but would push his son towards a trade. His hope is to be kept as the reliable worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a judgement on all of us for chasing the easy dollar. I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other, because the government will make a mess of it. I wouldn't be marching, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished at the mine within the year, and there's nothing else round here but farms, and the farms have robots too. I don't know what a man like me does then. I'm not going to say that at church, but it's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Ruth's father and ask if we could move onto the farm and work for our keep, he's got the old house standing empty. I'd sell what we could, the boat, the second truck. I'd lean on the church for a while, which I'd hate, but I'd do it for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. Like being underground when the lights go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate leaning on the church. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've always been the one carrying the casserole, not getting it. My father never took a handout in his life. But he never had to watch a robot do his job either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about government support? Would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to the kids going hungry, yes, I'd take it and keep quiet about it. I'd rather work for it, even sweeping the church hall. A man needs something to get up for.

S2.say: He'd call it a judgement on everyone for chasing easy money and say families and churches will have to carry each other since government would make a mess of it. He wouldn't march.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be finished at the mine within a year, with only farms nearby and those automated too. He doesn't know what he'd do and wouldn't say so at church.
S2.do: Asks Ruth's father whether the family can move into the empty house on his farm and work for their keep. Sells the boat and second truck, and leans on the church for a while for the children's sake.
S2.feel: Panicked, like being underground when the lights go out.
S2.quote: Because I've always been the one carrying the casserole, not getting it.
S2.fieldNote: Sam's pride is clear: he would accept help only for his children and would rather work for it. His fallback is family and church, not the state. The gap between what he'd say at church and what he feels is wide in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for a man to get his house in order. I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and look after their own. That's what I'd tell the men at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at forty-eight with the mortgage still hanging over us. I'd keep driving as long as they'd let me, and I'd probably fool myself it won't come to our mine. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the card and put fifty a fortnight away. I'd get Caleb signed up for an apprenticeship the day he's old enough. Ruth might ask the bakery for more hours. I'd keep my shuttle car clean and my record clean, and hope that counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, under the surface. It's a slow dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fool yourself. What would it take to wake you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing them bring the first automatic car down the ramp. When the milking robot came in, I knew the minute I saw it unloaded. Until then I'd tell myself the company's too cheap to buy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your record counted for nothing, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it'd be Ruth's father's farm, same as before, only we'd have had five years to get ready. Maybe I'd learn to fix fences and the pump properly, so I'm worth something there. Hands still count on a farm, for a while.

S3.say: He'd say five years is long enough for a man to put his house in order and urge workmates to look after their own rather than wait for government.
S3.think: He thinks he'd be forty-eight with the mortgage still unpaid. He'd keep driving as long as allowed and admits he'd probably tell himself it won't reach his mine.
S3.do: Pays down the credit card and saves fifty a fortnight. Signs his son up for an apprenticeship as soon as possible, while Ruth seeks more bakery hours and he keeps a clean work record.
S3.feel: Alarmed under the surface, a slow dread.
S3.quote: When the milking robot came in, I knew the minute I saw it unloaded.
S3.fieldNote: Sam knows his own tendency to deny change until he sees the machine. The extra years go into saving, his son's apprenticeship and a fallback on the family farm. His values push him to self-reliance even though he expects to need family help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell the young ones to get trades and the older men to pay off their houses. And I'd say we should be backing apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three and maybe the mortgage nearly done if I stay on. I think I could ride it out, honestly, the mine moves slowly. It's the kids I'd be thinking of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and put every spare dollar on the mortgage. I'd make sure Caleb and Hannah both go into something with a future, a trade for him, nursing maybe for her. I'd still stay away from the AI, I'd leave that to the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a quieter one. Ten years is a long time in a man's life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's twelve and she's the clever one. Her teacher says she could go to university. If there's a decade, I'd want her done with something solid before the robots arrive, and I'd go without to make it happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from AI. Even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got this far without it. I'm not saying it's evil, I'm saying it's not for me. Caleb can show me if I really need it.

S4.say: He'd call ten years fair warning, tell younger workers to learn trades and older ones to pay off their houses, and back apprenticeships over handouts.
S4.think: He thinks he could ride out the decade, as the mine moves slowly, reaching fifty-three with the mortgage nearly paid. His main concern is his children.
S4.do: Keeps driving and puts every spare dollar towards the mortgage. Steers his son into a trade and supports his daughter towards nursing or university, while still avoiding AI himself.
S4.feel: A quieter anxiety, since ten years is a long time in his life.
S4.quote: I've got this far without it. I'm not saying it's evil, I'm saying it's not for me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sam's focus moves almost entirely to his children's futures. He is still firmly against using AI himself but doesn't condemn it. Paying down the mortgage is his main financial goal, consistent with his self-reliant values.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no doubt. There'd be no time to get the house paid down or the kids set up, and nowhere round here to go. What would help is real work, even if it's lower pay, and apprenticeships for the young ones. I'd want to earn my way, not be paid to stay home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what work means to a man. It's not just the money. It's getting up in the dark and knowing your family is fed because of you.

headlineQuote: It's getting up in the dark and knowing your family is fed because of you.
portrait: Sam Baker is a 43-year-old shuttle car driver at a large underground potash mine, two years in after twenty years milking cows on a dairy that replaced him with a milking robot. His wife Ruth works mornings at a bakery, so his pay carries the family and there's nothing left over. He is traditional, church-going and self-reliant, and never uses AI. He's calm when nothing changes, anxious in the gradual picture and panicked in the two-year AGI picture, when he'd move to his father-in-law's farm. With more time he focuses on paying the mortgage and steering his children into trades and study.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to pay down the house or set up the kids, and nowhere nearby to go.
whatWouldHelp: Real work, even at lower pay, and apprenticeships for young people, so he can earn his way rather than be paid to stay home.
